description: if/else decisions and for/while loops — make your code choose and repeat.

screens.body:
An if statement runs code only when something is true. You write the condition, end the line with a colon, and indent the code that should run.

Think of it as a bouncer at a door: the indented block only gets in when the condition says yes.

options: Only when the condition is true
check.question: When does the indented block under an if run?

screens.heading: Code that makes decisions
screens.keyPoint: if + condition + colon — the indented block runs only when true.

screens.body:
Real decisions have more than two outcomes. elif means "else if" — it checks another condition when the first one was false. else catches everything left over.

Python checks them top to bottom and runs the first one that's true, then skips the rest.
screens.heading: else and elif
screens.keyPoint: elif checks the next condition; else catches everything left.

screens.body:
Conditions are built with comparison operators: == means equal, != means not equal, and > < >= <= compare sizes.

The classic beginner bug: using one = (which stores a value) when you meant == (which compares). if age = 18 doesn't ask a question — it tries to assign, and Python complains.
screens.heading: Comparing things
screens.keyPoint: == compares, = assigns — mixing them up is the classic bug.

screens.body:
Python has no curly braces. Instead, indentation — the spaces at the start of a line — marks which code belongs to the if, loop, or function above it.

Use 4 spaces per level. If your indentation is off, Python either errors out or runs code you didn't mean to run. When something weird happens, check your spaces first.

check.question: What marks a block of code in Python?

code.snippet:
hungry = True
if hungry:
    print("Time to eat")
    print("Making jollof...")
print("Done")

screens.heading: Indentation is the rule
screens.keyPoint: Indent with 4 spaces — Python has no braces.

screens.body:
A for loop repeats once for each item in a sequence. for name in names runs the block once per name — the loop variable holds the current item each round.

range(5) is a handy counter: it gives you 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Note it stops before 5 — range always stops one short of the number you give it.
screens.heading: for loops: repeat for each item
screens.keyPoint: for ... in ... repeats once per item; range(n) counts 0 to n-1.

screens.body:
A while loop repeats as long as its condition stays true — perfect when you don't know how many rounds you need. "Keep going while the battery is above 20%."

The golden rule: something inside the loop must move the condition toward false. If it never becomes false, the loop runs forever — an infinite loop.

options: The condition must be able to turn false
It must contain a for loop
check.question: What must happen inside a while loop?

code.snippet:
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n = n - 1

screens.heading: while loops: repeat until false
screens.keyPoint: while repeats while its condition is true — always move toward false.

screens.body:
Sometimes you need to bail out of a loop early or skip a round. break exits the loop completely — you're done, move on. continue skips the rest of this round and jumps to the next one.

They're small words with big control. Use them when the loop's normal ending isn't quite what you want.
screens.heading: break and continue
screens.keyPoint: break quits the loop; continue skips one round.

screens.body: The official tutorial's control-flow chapter (docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html) covers everything here — if, for, while, break, continue — with more examples. For the exact rules, the compound statements reference (docs.python.org/3/reference/compound_stmts.html) has the full details.
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: The official docs are your best next stop.
